domains.title: Island of the Eighty-Eight Temples
domains.subtitle: Pilgrimage, Rural Japan, and the Cult of Kūkai
domains.lead: Shikoku is Japan's smallest main island, a place of mountains, coast, and rural quiet. For more than a thousand years it has been walked by pilgrims on the henro, the 88-temple circuit associated with Kūkai, the founder of Shingon Buddhism. Shikoku means 'four provinces,' and its identity is inseparable from the spiritual geography of the pilgrimage.

mythology.lead: Shikoku's mythology is the mythology of Kūkai and the Buddhist pilgrimage that bears his memory.

myths.title: Kūkai and Shingon
myths.text: Kūkai (774–835), posthumously known as Kōbō Daishi, was born in Sanuki province on Shikoku. He founded the Shingon school of esoteric Buddhism, established the monastery on Mount Kōya, and is credited with countless legends. After his death, he was believed to remain in eternal meditation, guiding pilgrims who walk the 88 temples.

myths.title: The Eighty-Eight Temples
myths.text: The Shikoku Henro links 88 temples associated with Kūkai's life and practice. Pilgrims walk clockwise around the island, often in the traditional white robes and sedge hat. The journey is understood as a symbolic rebirth and a walking meditation in Kūkai's presence.

myths.title: Kūkai as Living Presence
myths.text: Many pilgrims believe that Kūkai walks the henro with them, appearing as a helpful stranger, a child, or a beggar. This belief transforms the pilgrimage from a historical commemoration into an ongoing encounter with the sacred.

lore.syncretism: Shikoku blends Buddhism, Shinto, and folk religion along the pilgrimage route. Shinto shrines sit beside Buddhist temples, and local kami are honored as manifestations of Buddhist figures. The island's identity is so bound up with Kūkai and the henro that pilgrimage and place are nearly synonymous.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Shikoku Henro remains one of Japan's most important pilgrimages, attracting walkers from across the country and abroad. The island's rural culture, udon noodles, and natural scenery are celebrated in travel writing and media. Shikoku represents a slower, more contemplative Japan.
lore.extendedMeditation: Shikoku teaches that a place can become sacred through walking. The island is not merely the setting of the pilgrimage; the pilgrimage is the island's true form. To walk the henro is to let the land shape the soul.

sources.name: Reader, Making Pilgrimages: Meaning and Practice in Shikoku

lore.archaeology: The Shikoku Henro circuit preserves temples from the Heian period to the present, many associated with Kūkai's legend. Mount Kōya, though technically in Wakayama, is the spiritual center of the Shingon tradition and a UNESCO World Heritage site linked to Shikoku's pilgrimage culture.
